analytic.title: FGL2 <sub>172-220</sub> peptides improve the antitumor effect of HCMV-IE1mut vaccine against glioblastoma by modulating immunosuppressive cells in the tumor microenvironment

div.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a highly aggressive primary brain tumor characterized by poor prognosis and lack of effective treatments. In recent years, peptide vaccines that use sequences based on tumor-specific or tumor-associated antigens to activate immune responses against tumor cells have emerged as a new therapeutic strategy. In this study, we developed a novel therapeutic polypeptide vaccine targeting the tumor-associated antigen Fibrinogen-Like Protein 2 (FGL2), whose dominant epitope peptide was tandemly linked to the C-terminus of HCMV-IE1mut via a linker. We used this vaccine to compare the therapeutic efficacy of HCMV-IE1mut alone versus HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 and investigate the potential mechanism of action of HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 in glioma treatment. An in situ GBM model (GL261-IE1-luc cells) was used to determine the efficacy of the vaccine. Treatment with HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 exerted antitumor effects and extended the survival of the GL261 animal model. We observed reduced proportions of microglia, regulatory T cells (Treg), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) in the tumor microenvironment (TME) by immunofluorescence. Flow cytometry showed that compared to HCMV-IE1mut alone, treatment with HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 increased the proportion of CD8+ T cells and tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM). ELISA analysis showed that it improved the secretion of tumor-specific IFN-γ and TNF-α by these cells and downregulated the expression of IL-6 and IL-10. Our study demonstrates that the long-peptide FGL2 172-220 improves the antitumor efficacy of HCMV-IE1mut, possibly by reshaping immune cells in the glioma microenvironment. These findings lay the groundwork for the development of therapeutic antigenic peptide vaccines to improve antitumor effects for cancer.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common primary brain tumor in adults with potent immunosuppressive properties. 1 Conventional therapies for gliomas include surgical excision as well as a combination of radiation therapy and adjuvant temozolomide. 2,3 Nevertheless, the rapid growth, invasive behavior, and complex genomic characteristics of glioma restrict the therapeutic effect. This is particularly true for highly aggressive glioblastoma multiforme, wherein patient life expectancy is extended to no more than 16 months. 4 Recent advances in molecularly targeted therapies and immunotherapy have initiated a new era of GBM therapy, utilizing the immune system to identify and eradicate cancerous cells. To improve the prognosis of GBM, efforts have been made to understand the immune response and immune microenvironment of the disease. 5 Regretfully, clinical trials have shown that immune checkpoint blockade therapies targeting the immune microenvironment of the tumor have limited efficacy in GBM. 6 Therefore, it is imperative to develop novel therapeutic approaches to enhance patient outcomes.

Tumor vaccines are promising options to replace or assist traditional therapies to improve efficacy. An increasing amount of clinical research has indicated the significant role of tumor vaccines in enhancing patient survival. 7,8 The tumor vaccines based on peptides have a promising new avenue for study. An antitumor peptide vaccine can remodel the tumor microenvironment (TME) and promote antitumor immunity. 9 Multiepitope tumor peptides, in contrast to short-peptide vaccines, require internalization and processing by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) before presentation. 10 By targeting specific antigens on the surface of tumor cells, peptide vaccines are designed to induce a strong and durable immune response that can eliminate tumor cells with minimal damage to healthy cells.

Fibrinogen-like protein 2 (FGL2) is a tumor-associated antigen that is intimately linked to the development of various cancers. It promotes breast tumor progression by increasing tumor angiogenesis or inducing epithelial-mesenchymal transition 11 ; In hepatocellular carcinoma, FGL2 promotes the development and spread of tumor by inhibiting T-cell activation and improving the immune escape of tumor cells 12 ; It promotes tumor growth by attenuating the infiltration of activated immune cells in melanoma and ovarian cancer models. 13 In recent years, FGL2 has been identified for the first time as a promoter of glioblastoma progression and transition from lowgrade astrocytoma to high-grade glioblastoma. 14,15 FGL2 achieves immunosuppression in cancer by inhibiting APC activity, reducing T-cell proliferation, and activating regulatory T-cell (Treg) function. 16,17 Based on its differential expression in glioma and normal tissues, we developed a peptide vaccine targeting FGL2. As mentioned earlier, multiepitope long-peptide vaccines provide greater benefits than short-peptide vaccines. Therefore, our goal was to design a comprehensive multiepitope long-peptide vaccine focused on FGL2. However, the short in vivo half-life and low immunogenicity of peptide vaccines restrict their biological effects, as they cannot induce a strong immune response when administered alone; hence, carrier proteins are generally required to improve the effects of antigenic peptide-specific immune responses. Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) proteins were initially identified in GBM more than 20 years ago. 18 Subsequently, sufficient evidence has demonstrated the majority of glioblastomas have HCMV sequences and express the genes. 19 We previously, used the HCMV immediate early protein IE1 to treat glioma. However, due to the immunotoxicity of the viral protein IE1, we developed the IE1 mutant vaccine (IE1mut) to ensure vaccine safety. This mutant effectively activated the in vivo immune response and exhibited good antitumor activity. 20 Nonetheless, the presence of immunosuppressive cells in the TME limits the effectiveness of single-antigen antitumor therapy.

On the basis of this foundation, we screened potential long peptides targeting FGL2 using bioinformatics methods. To improve their immunogenicity and prevent rapid degradation in vivo, we coupled these peptides with HCMV-IE1mut via prokaryotic expression and investigated their immune and antitumor effects in vivo. Our results demonstrated that peptides vaccine FGL2 172-220 effectively inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival, established long-term immune memory, and augmented the antitumor effect of HCMV-IE1mut by remodeling immune cells in the tumor immune microenvironment. This development model facilitates the effective screening of multiple target antigens and provides novel perspectives on peptide vaccines targeting tumor-associated antigens.

div.head: peptide couplers
div.p: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database indicates that glioma patients have high expression levels of FGL2 (Figure 1a). We confirmed increased mFGL2 expression in brain tissues of GL261 tumor-bearing mice via qPCR compared to healthy mice (Figure 1b) and designed a tumor peptide vaccine targeting mFGL2. Multiple potentially advantageous epitopes of FGL2 protein were predicted by DNAstar, IEDB, and SOPMA (Figure 1c,d). Tables S1-S3 present the candidate peptide scores according to B-cell antigenicity, Th-cell epitopes, and CTL cellular epitopes. We predicted and screened two FGL2-derived peptides: FGL2 172-220 and FGL2 350-398 . To enhance recognition of them by the immune system, we mixed the peptides with the MF59 adjuvant and injected them into wild-type mice (Supplementary Figure S1A). Following three weekly injections in wild-type mice, we found that FGL2 172-220 more effectively activated dendritic cells and macrophages than FGL2 350-398 (Supplementary Figure S1B-E). We preliminarily conclude that FGL2 172-220 is recognized by the host immune system and is capable of enhancing antigen presentation capacity. Based on these results, we selected FGL2 172-220 (NLTVVVNSLDGKCSKCPSQEHMQSQPVQHLIYKDCSD-HYVLGRRSSGAY) as the candidate peptide.

HCMV is a β-herpesvirus, and the IE1 protein is its immediate early protein. Considering the effect of IE1 on virus replication forks and the immunotoxicity it carries, we further developed a mutated form of IE1 protein (IE1mut) to lessen any possible risk to human. We mutated five sites, K223A, N237A, N285A, M296A, and R310A, 21 based on the sequence of the IE1 protein to obtain HCMV-IE1mut as these sites are closely related to the restart of stalled viral replication. Preliminary laboratory experiments have demonstrated that HCMV-IE1mut exhibits promising anti-glioma activity. Conjugating it with the FGL2 172-220 peptide effectively prevents peptide degradation and ensures efficient recognition of the half-antigen by APCs. To improve the coupling efficiency, we performed protein purification using a prokaryotic expression system. WB analysis revealed obvious protein bands between 60 and 80 kDa (Figure 1e,f), which confirmed the coupling of FGL2 172-220 with HCMV-IE1-mut and its successful purification.

div.head: The HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine exerted no serious toxic side effects in mice
div.p: To evaluate the safety of the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine, each group of mice received three intramuscular immunizations on days 0, 7, and 14, with a dose of 20 µg of the HCMV-IE1mut or HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine (Figure 2a). Serum biochemical parameters were investigated in each group of mice one day after the third immunization. Major tissues were also subjected to H&E staining. The results of both H&E staining (Figure 2b) and biochemical parameter measurements (Figure 2c) from each group remained within normal ranges. Except for a slight increase in alveolar thickness in the treated mice. Overall, this indicated that the FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine did not induce significant toxic side effects in mice.

div.head: FGL2 172-220 peptide improved the antitumor activity of HCMV-IE1mut in vivo and prolonged the survival of GL261 animal model
div.p: To explore the antitumor effect of HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 in vivo, we established an orthotopic glioma model in C57BL/ 6J mice by injecting 5 × 10 4 GL261-IE1-luc cells into the brain. After successful tumor establishment, the mice were randomly assigned into PBS, HCMV-IE1mut, and HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment groups. Treatments were administered via intramuscular injections at specified time points, with booster immunizations performed on days 14 and 21 after the inoculation of tumor cells (Figure 3a). The mice were tracked weekly to determine any changes in body weight during the course of the medication. Mice in the control group exhibited a significant decrease in average body weight as tumors progressed; however, mice treated with HCMV-IE1mut or HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 exhibited no significant changes in body weight (Figure 3b). Tumor growth in the brain before each vaccine injection was evaluated using real-time imaging techniques. Bioluminescence imaging revealed no significant difference in tumor size between the groups after the first injection. However, after the second immunization, tumors in the HCMV-IE1mut or HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment groups exhibited significant growth inhibition. After the third injection, tumors in the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment group exhibited more pronounced regression than those in the HCMV-IE1mut alone treatment group (Figure 3c,d). These findings were confirmed by histological examination of H&E-stained brain tissues (Figure 3e). We also found that mice in the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment group had more tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. Remarkably, in this vaccine group, the infiltrating lymphocytes were "repelling" tumor cells that had spread in the adjacent brain tissue (Figure 3e,f). We next recorded the survival of mice and found a significantly increased survival rate among mice in the HCMV-IE1mut or HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment group compared with that among control mice (Figure 3g). 4a). Therefore, we suggest that the FGL2 172-220 peptide does not directly regulate the proliferation of glioma cells, but it rather affects the TME to promote the antitumor effect of IE1mut.

Based on the role of TAM (Tumor-associated macrophage) and GAM (Glioma-associated microglia and macrophages) in gliomas, 22 we found that with the FGL2 172-220 peptide virtually eliminated the presence of microglia by immunofluorescence staining for the microglia surface marker IBA. Furthermore, there was a decrease in the proportion of CD206 + cells, suggesting that the FGL2 172-220 peptide improved the TME (Figure 4b,c). GME (Glioma microenvironment) is characterized by the accumulation of high levels of Tregs and MDSCs. 23,24 Through flow cytometry, we detected the presence of CD4 + T cells and Treg cells in the Glioblastoma tissues of control and treated animals. Treatment with HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 induced higher levels of CD4 + T cells within the TME (Figure 4d-f) and fewer Treg cells, whereas treatment with IE1mut alone did not reduce the proportion of Treg cells in brain tumors. This result was consistent with the results of lymphocytes from spleen and lymph nodes (Figure 4g-j). This suggests that the vaccine exerts a similar regulatory effect on immune cells in peripheral immune organs. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a type of tumor-infiltrating innate immune cells. Our flow cytometry experiments with relevant membrane markers (CD11b and Gr-1) revealed a significant reduction in the proportion of MDSCs was significantly reduced in the peptide treatment group, whereas there was no difference between the HCMV-IE1mut treatment and control group (Figure 4k). Moreover, these findings were supported by immunostaining (Figure 4l). Altogether, these data suggest that the FGL2 172-220 peptide inhibits the infiltration of immunosuppressive cells in the TME.

div.head: FGL2 172-220 peptide-induced CD8+ T cells to be recruited into the TME and to generate tumor-specific brainresident memory T cells
div.p: Based on the above findings and considering that MDSCs and M2 macrophages are the main cell types restricting T cell entry into tumor tissue, 25 we further investigated CD8+ T cell infiltration in the TME. Results showed that the FGL2 172-220 peptide improved the aggregation and infiltration of T lymphocytes in tumors (Figure 5a,b), and this finding was also confirmed by immunofluorescence (Figure 5c). CD8 + T cells that migrate to non-lymphoid tissues during the immune response receive signals from the local microenvironment that promote their retention in the tissue and differentiation into tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM). 26 We also found a significant increase in the proportion of TRMs in the tumors of mice treated with HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 , whereas no difference was found between the PBS and HCMV-IE1mut treatment groups; this result was also confirmed in the spleen (Figure 5d-f).

Next, we investigated the proportion of effector memory T cells (TEM) and central-type memory T cells (TCM) as they play a vital role in secreting cytokines to kill tumor cells. Our results demonstrated that the FGL2 172-220 peptide induced specific CD8 + T cells in the spleen predominantly exhibiting an effector memory cell phenotype, whereas in lymphoid tissues, they primarily exhibited a central memory phenotype. Meanwhile, we found that after HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment, the proportion of central-type memory T (TCM) cells in lymphoid tissues increased from 18.4% to 36.64%, whereas that of the effector memory-like phenotype (TEM) decreased from 21.14% to 10.34% (Figure 5g,h). This result suggests that the FGL2 172-220 peptide induces long-term immunity in the periphery and that it would reverse the effect of HCMV-IE1mut-induced differentiation of CD8 + T cells into TEM into the differentiation of more TCM.

div.head: FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine induced robust antigenspecific CTL responses and innate immune responses in vivo
div.p: To explore whether the FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine induced cellular immune responses in vivo to exert antitumor effects, we isolated splenic lymphocytes of mouse bearing GL261 tumor after being immunized with three injections for flow assay analysis. We discovered that there were noticeably more CD8+ T and CD4+ T cells in the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine-treated group compared with HCMV-IE1-mut alone (Figure 6a,b). Our results also demonstrated significantly increased expression of IFN-γ and TNF-α in these cells in the HCMV-IE1mut and HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 vaccinetreated groups, with the increase being more pronounced in the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 vaccine-treated group (Figure 6c,d). Serum analysis by ELISA also revealed elevated levels of IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2 and decreased levels of IL-6 and IL-10 in mice treated with the vaccines compared with that in the control group (Figure 6e). These data suggest that the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 vaccine induced the differentiation of Th0 cells into Th1 cells, driving T-cell polarization toward a Th1 effector phenotype, thereby exerting antitumor effects.

We also noted stimulation of the mice's innate immune system. For instance, after the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide treatment, dendritic cells were activated, as indicated by increased expression of activation markers such as CD80, CD86, MHC-I, and MHC-II (Figure 6f). These markers are associated with antigen presentation and immune cell immunofluorescence. (g-j) Detection of treg cell ratios in spleen, lymph nodes, and tumors by flow cytometry. These findings suggest that the FGL2 172-220 peptide vaccine not only promotes the cytotoxic function of T cells but also activates innate immunity.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Polypeptide vaccines utilizing antigenic dominant epitopes provide a compelling therapeutic choice because of their safety, easy production, and user-friendly nature compared with conventional vaccines. 28 Ideally, candidate tumor antigens for cancer vaccines must exhibit high expression in the tumor tissue. 29 In this study, a bioinformatics approach was used to predict antigenically dominant epitopes of FGL2, based on which we designed a glioma long peptide vaccine. Nevertheless, peptides exert a limited biological effect due to their short half-life in the body and low immunogenicity, preventing them from sufficiently stimulating a robust immune response independently. 30 The high expression of HCMV IE1 protein in glioma tissues is closely related to the development of invasive gliomas. 31 And we have previously shown that HCMV-IE1mut can cause a strong reaction in the body to exert antitumor effects. 20 Based on the characteristics of HCMV-IE1mut and FGL2 peptides, we designed the HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 peptide tumor vaccine for treating the GL261 tumor. In assessing the vaccine's safety, we discovered that the mice in the vaccine-treated group had a little increase in alveolar thickness. This outcome is consistent with earlier research 32 and is typically brought on by immune system activation.

GAMs are typically considered to promote tumorigenesis, and their presence in the TME is frequently associated with unfavorable outcomes and a poor prognosis for patients with glioma. 33 FGL2 172-220 reduces microglial infiltration to some extent and decreases the M2 polarization of glioma-associated microglia, supporting its tumor-killing immune response. It has been previously shown that FGL2 promotes Treg activity, inhibits Th1 response, improves Th2 tilt, and downregulates antigen-presenting activity. 34 Consistent with this, treatment with the FGL2 172-220 peptide reduced Treg lymphocyte expansion and induced Th0 differentiation in the periphery with a bias toward the Th1 immune response. Targeting tumor-associated MDSCs in the microenvironment is another therapeutic approach for treating gliomas. 35 Our immunofluorescence results were consistent with those of flow cytometry assays, and HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 treatment significantly reduced the proportion of MDSCs, whereas no difference was found between HCMV-IE1mut and control treatments. Based on these results and those of previous research, 36 we speculate that the reduction in the proportion of M2-type microglia reduces the expression of cytokines or chemokines (e.g., IL-10, TGF-β, IL-4, IL-6, CCL2, CCL5, and CCL20), which in turn reduces the aggregation of immune-suppressing cells; however, this speculation must be further verified at a later stage.

CD4 + T-cell assistance is a key aspect of CD8 + T-cell activation and tumor immunity. 37 Based on the detection of TNF-α and IFN-γ, we believe that FGL2 172-220 can improve the tumorkilling effect of CTLs through these cytokines. CD4 T cells can also facilitate the activation and maturation of DCs, promoting the expression of costimulatory molecules and the secretion of cytokines essential for inducing DC maturation, which in turn contributes to the priming of CD8 T cells. 38 This study demonstrated through ELISA that the cytokine essential for inducing DC maturation is IL-2. NK cells also perform a comparable function. 39 Based on the activation of DC and NK cells in mice treated with IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 , there is collaborative evidence suggesting that CD4 T cells work with NK cells and DCs to induce CD8 T-cell priming.

Compared with that by HCMV-IE1mut treatment, HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment induced higher levels of TEM and TCM in the spleen, with a predominance of TEM. Interestingly, unlike that in the spleen, FGL2 172-220 induced more TCM as well as less TEM in lymph nodes. Based on these previous studies, we speculate that the FGL2 172-220 peptide induces more TCM in lymph nodes because the immune system is more reinforced to memorize specific antigens after vaccination, and TCM may return to the lymph nodes via efferent lymphatics, thoracic ducts, and the bloodstream. 40 Instead, less TEM levels are induced because the body has already eliminated most of the antigen and no longer needs to maintain high levels of effector memory T cells in response to continued antigen exposure. In fact, TCM undergoes significant expansion upon reencountering pathogens, surpassing other memory T cells in generating secondary T-cell responses. 41 More recently, TRM populations have also been reported in the brain. 42 We found that HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 treatment induced TRM production, whereas the result of HCMV-IE1mut treatment was not different from that in the PBS group. Tissue-retention molecules expressed by TRMs inhibit the egress of memory T cells from tissues. 43 Therefore, we propose that the long-peptide FGL2 172- 220 inhibits the depletion of memory T cells in tumors by promoting TRM formation, thereby augmenting the function of IE1mut-induced CD8 T cells.

Our study has certain limitations. The TME in GBM is intricate and influenced by both external components and intrinsic mechanisms of the tumor itself. 44 In addition, the growth and evolution of human gliomas cannot be accurately simulated in our animal models. While we have seen an increase in CD8+ cells inside the tumor, we are still unsure of the exact method by which peripheral immune cells penetrate the blood-brain barrier. Subsequent investigations may concentrate on this process, in addition to enhancing the flexibility of animal models to more accurately replicate the environment of human gliomas and assess the anticancer properties of peripheral immune cells.

To summarize, we demonstrated that HCMV-IE1mut-FGL2 172-220 exhibited significant and sustained antitumor efficacy in mice bearing GL261 tumors, and further experiments revealed that the long-peptide FGL2 172-220 synergistically improved the antitumor efficacy of IE1mut by inducing CD8 + T cells as well as by remodeling immune-suppressor cells in the glioma microenvironment. Our work ultimately advances the development of tumor immunotherapy techniques and offers a useful resource for future research on tailored tumor vaccines.
